278+-- ### Assertion Implication
279+
280+-- Given two assertions `P` and `Q`, we say that `P` *implies* `Q`, written
281+-- `P ->> Q`, if, whenever `P` holds in some state `st`, `Q` also holds.
282+
283+def AssertImplies (P Q : Assertion) : Prop :=
284+  ∀ st, P st → Q st
285+
286+-- Note that the notation for *assertion implication* is analogous to the
287+-- "usual" Lean implication `→`.
288+
289+notation:26 P:27 " ->> " Q:27 => AssertImplies P Q
290+
291+theorem assertImplies_def {P Q : Assertion} : P ->> Q ↔ ∀ st, P st → Q st := by rfl
292+
293+-- We'll also want the "iff" variant of implication between assertions:
294+
295+notation:26 P:27 " <<->> " Q:27 => AssertImplies P Q ∧ AssertImplies Q P
296+
297+-- ## Hoare Triples, Informally
298+
299+-- A *Hoare triple* is a claim about the state before and after executing a
300+-- command. The standard notation is
301+
302+--   {P} c {Q}
303+
304+-- meaning:
305+
306+-- - If command `c` begins execution in a state satisfying assertion `P`,
307+-- - and if `c` eventually terminates in some final state,
308+-- - then that final state will satisfy the assertion `Q`.
309+
310+-- Assertion `P` is called the *precondition* of the triple, and `Q` is the
311+-- *postcondition*.
312+
313+-- Because single braces are already used for other things in Lean, we'll
314+-- write Hoare triples with double braces:
315+
316+--   {{P}} c {{Q}}
317+
318+-- For example,
319+
320+-- - The Hoare triple
321+
322+--   {{X = 0}} X := X + 1 {{X = 1}}
323+
324+-- states that command `X := X + 1` will transform a state in which `X = 0` to
325+-- a state in which `X = 1`.
326+
327+-- - On the other hand,
328+
329+--   ∀ m, {{X = m}} X := X + 1 {{X = m + 1}}
330+
331+-- is a *proposition* stating that the Hoare triple
332+-- `{{X = m}} X :=
333+-- X + 1 {{X = m + 1}}` is valid for any choice of `m`. Note
334+-- that `m` in the two assertions is a reference to the *Lean* variable `m`,
335+-- which is bound outside the Hoare triple.
336+
337+-- _Quiz:_
338+

340+
341+--   1) {{True}} c {{X = 5}}
342+
343+--   2) ∀ m, {{X = m}} c {{X = m + 5}}
344+
345+--   3) {{X ≤ Y}} c {{Y ≤ X}}
346+
347+--   4) {{True}} c {{False}}
348+
349+--   5) ∀ m,
350+--        {{X = m}}
351+--        c
352+--        {{Y = real_fact m}}
353+
354+--   6) ∀ m,
355+--        {{X = m}}
356+--        c
357+--        {{(Z * Z) ≤ m ∧ ¬ ((Z + 1) * (Z + 1) ≤ m)}}
358+

481+-- ## Hoare Triples, Formally
482+
483+-- We formalize valid Hoare triples in Lean as follows:
484+
485+def ValidHoareTriple
486+    (P : Assertion) (c : Com) (Q : Assertion) : Prop :=
487+  ∀ st st',
488+    (st =[ c ]=> st') →
489+    P st →
490+    Q st'
491+
492+-- Notation for Hoare triples. The command between the two assertions is
493+-- parsed with the same grammar as the `imp { … }` notation, so a command that
494+-- is a Lean variable (rather than concrete syntax) is spliced in with `~c`,
495+-- just as in the `st =[ c ]=> st'` notation.
496+
497+open scoped Assertion
498+
499+namespace ValidHoareTriple
500+
501+/-- Hoare triple: `{{ P }} c {{ Q }}` -/
502+scoped syntax:lead "{{" term "}} " imp_com:lead " {{" term "}}" : term
503+
504+macro_rules
505+  | `({{ $P }} $c:imp_com {{ $Q }}) =>
506+      `(ValidHoareTriple ({{ $P }}) (imp { $c }) ({{ $Q }}))
507+
508+end ValidHoareTriple
509+
510+section
511+open scoped ValidHoareTriple

531+-- ## Proof Rules
532+
533+-- The goal of Hoare logic is to provide a *compositional* method for proving
534+-- the validity of specific Hoare triples. That is, we want the structure of a
535+-- program's correctness proof to mirror the structure of the program itself.
536+-- To this end, in the sections below, we'll introduce a rule for reasoning
537+-- about each of the different syntactic forms of commands in Imp -- one for
538+-- assignment, one for sequencing, one for conditionals, etc. -- plus a couple
539+-- of "structural" rules for gluing things together. We will then be able to
540+-- prove programs correct using these proof rules, without ever unfolding the
541+-- definition of `ValidHoareTriple`.
542+
543+-- ### Skip
544+
545+-- Since `skip` doesn't change the state, it preserves any assertion `P`:
546+
547+--   --------------------  (hoare_skip)
548+--   {{ P }} skip {{ P }}
549+
550+theorem hoare_skip (P : Assertion) :
551+    {{ P }} skip; {{ P }} := by
552+  intro st st' h hp
553+  inversion h
554+  assumption
555+
556+-- ### Sequencing
557+
558+-- If command `c1` takes any state where `P` holds to a state where `Q` holds,
559+-- and if `c2` takes any state where `Q` holds to one where `R` holds, then
560+-- doing `c1` followed by `c2` will take any state where `P` holds to one
561+-- where `R` holds:
562+
563+--    {{ P }} c1 {{ Q }}
564+--    {{ Q }} c2 {{ R }}
565+--   ----------------------  (hoare_seq)
566+--   {{ P }} c1;c2 {{ R }}
567+
568+theorem hoare_seq (P Q R : Assertion) (c1 c2 : Com)
569+    (h1 : {{ Q }} ~c2 {{ R }}) (h2 : {{ P }} ~c1 {{ Q }}) :
570+    {{ P }} ~c1 ~c2 {{ R }} := by
571+  intro st st' h12 pre
572+  inversion h12 with
573+  | seq st'' hc1 hc2 =>
574+    exact h1 _ _ hc2 (h2 _ _ hc1 pre)
575+
576+-- Note that, in the formal rule `hoare_seq`, the premises are given in
577+-- backwards order (`c2` before `c1`). This matches the natural flow of
578+-- information in many of the situations where we'll use the rule, since the
579+-- natural way to construct a Hoare-logic proof is to begin at the end of the
580+-- program (with the final postcondition) and push postconditions backwards
581+-- through commands until we reach the beginning.
582+
583+-- ### Assignment
584+
585+-- The rule for assignment is the most fundamental of the Hoare logic proof
586+-- rules. Here's how it works.
587+
588+-- Consider this incomplete Hoare triple:
589+
590+--   {{ ??? }}  X := Y  {{ X = 1 }}
591+
592+-- We want to assign `Y` to `X` and finish in a state where `X` is `1`. What
593+-- could the precondition be?
594+
595+-- One possibility is `Y = 1`, because if `Y` is already `1` then assigning it
596+-- to `X` causes `X` to be `1`. That leads to a valid Hoare triple:
597+
598+--   {{ Y = 1 }}  X := Y  {{ X = 1 }}
599+
600+-- It may seem as though coming up with that precondition must have taken some
601+-- clever thought. But there is a mechanical way we could have done it: if we
602+-- take the postcondition `X = 1` and in it replace `X` with `Y`---that is,
603+-- replace the left-hand side of the assignment statement with the right-hand
604+-- side---we get the precondition, `Y = 1`.
605+
606+-- That same idea works in more complicated cases. For example:
607+
608+--   {{ ??? }}  X := X + Y  {{ X = 1 }}
609+
610+-- If we replace the `X` in `X = 1` with `X + Y`, we get `X + Y = 1`. That
611+-- again leads to a valid Hoare triple:
612+
613+--   {{ X + Y = 1 }}  X := X + Y  {{ X = 1 }}
614+
615+-- Why does this technique work? The postcondition identifies some property
616+-- `P` that we want to hold of the variable `X` being assigned. In this case,
617+-- `P` is "equals `1`". To complete the triple and make it valid, we need to
618+-- identify a precondition that guarantees that property will hold of `X`.
619+-- Such a precondition must ensure that the same property holds of *whatever
620+-- is being assigned to* `X`. So, in the example, we need "equals `1`" to hold
621+-- of `X + Y`. That's exactly what the technique guarantees.
622+
623+-- In general, the postcondition could be some arbitrary assertion `Q`, and
624+-- the right-hand side of the assignment could be some arbitrary arithmetic
625+-- expression `a`:
626+
627+--   {{ ??? }}  X := a  {{ Q }}
628+
629+-- The precondition would then be `Q`, but with any occurrences of `X` in it
630+-- replaced by `a`.
631+
632+-- Let's introduce a notation for this idea of replacing occurrences: Define
633+-- `Q \[X ↦ a`] to mean "`Q` where `a` is substituted in place of `X`".
634+
635+-- This yields the Hoare logic rule for assignment:
636+
637+--   {{ Q [X ↦ a] }}  X := a  {{ Q }}
638+
639+-- One way of reading this rule is: If you want statement `X := a` to
640+-- terminate in a state that satisfies assertion `Q`, then it suffices to
641+-- start in a state that also satisfies `Q`, except where `a` is substituted
642+-- for every occurrence of `X`.
643+
644+-- To many people, this rule seems "backwards" at first, because it proceeds
645+-- from the postcondition to the precondition. Actually it makes good sense to
646+-- go in this direction: the postcondition is often what is more important,
647+-- because it characterizes what will be true after running the code.
648+
649+-- Nonetheless, it's also possible to formulate a "forward" assignment rule.
650+-- We'll do that later in some exercises.
651+
652+-- Here are some valid instances of the assignment rule:
653+
654+--   {{ (X ≤ 5) [X ↦ X + 1] }}         (that is, X + 1 ≤ 5)
655+--     X := X + 1
656+--   {{ X ≤ 5 }}
657+
658+--   {{ (X = 3) [X ↦ 3] }}              (that is, 3 = 3)
659+--     X := 3
660+--   {{ X = 3 }}
661+
662+--   {{ (0 ≤ X ∧ X ≤ 5) [X ↦ 3] }}.  (that is, 0 ≤ 3 ∧ 3 ≤ 5)
663+--     X := 3
664+--   {{ 0 ≤ X ∧ X ≤ 5 }}
665+
666+-- To formalize the rule, we must first formalize the idea of "substituting an
667+-- expression for an Imp variable in an assertion", which we refer to as
668+-- assertion substitution, or `Assertion.sub`.
669+
670+-- Intuitively, given a proposition `P`, a variable `X`, and an arithmetic
671+-- expression `a`, we want to derive another proposition `P'` that is just the
672+-- same as `P` except that `P'` should mention `a` wherever `P` mentions `X`.
673+
674+-- This operation is related to the idea of substituting Imp expressions for
675+-- Imp variables that we saw in *Equiv* (`subst_aexp` and friends). The
676+-- difference is that, here, `P` is an arbitrary Lean assertion, so we can't
677+-- directly "edit" its text.
678+
679+-- However, we can achieve the same effect by evaluating `P` in an updated
680+-- state, defined as follows:
681+
682+def Assertion.sub (x : Ident) (a : Aexp) (P : Assertion) : Assertion :=
683+  fun (st : State) => P (x →ₜ a.eval st ; st)
684+
685+/-- Assertion substitution: `P [X ↦ a]` -/
686+syntax:100 term:100 " [" ident " ↦ " imp_aexp "]" : term
687+
688+macro_rules
689+  | `($P [$x ↦ $a]) => `(Assertion.sub $x (aexp { $a }) $P)
690+  -- | `(assn($st; $P [$x ↦ $a])) => ``(assn($st; $P) [$x ↦ $a]) -- maybe we could push substitutions inside
691+
692+-- This notation allows us to write this operation as:
693+
694+--   P [ X ↦ a ]
695+
696+#check (fun st => Assertion.sub X (aexp { 2 * X }) ({{ X ≤ 10 }}) st)
697+#check {{ X ≤ 10 }} [X ↦ 2 * X]
698+#check (∀ st, ({{ X ≤ 10 }} [X ↦ 2 * X]) st)
699+
700+-- That is, `P [X ↦ a]` stands for an assertion -- let's call it `P'` -- that
701+-- behaves just like `P` except that, wherever `P` looks up the variable `X`
702+-- in the current state, `P'` instead uses the value of the expression `a`.
703+
704+-- To see how this works in more detail, let's calculate what happens with a
705+-- couple of examples. First, suppose `P'` is `(X ≤ 5) [X ↦ 3]` -- that is,
706+-- more formally, `P'` is the Lean expression
707+
708+--   fun st =>
709+--     (fun st' => st'[X] ≤ 5)
710+--     (X →ₜ Aexp.eval st 3 ; st),
711+
712+-- which simplifies to
713+
714+--   fun st =>
715+--     (fun st' => st'[X] ≤ 5)
716+--     (X →ₜ 3 ; st)
717+
718+-- and further simplifies to
719+
720+--   fun st =>
721+--     ((X →ₜ 3 ; st)[X]) ≤ 5
722+
723+-- and finally to
724+
725+--   fun st =>
726+--     3 ≤ 5.
727+
728+-- That is, `P'` is the assertion that `3` is less than or equal to `5` (as
729+-- expected).
730+
731+-- For a more interesting example, suppose `P'` is `(X ≤ 5) [X ↦
732+-- X + 1]`.
733+-- Formally, `P'` is the Lean expression
734+
735+--   fun st =>
736+--     (fun st' => st'[X] ≤ 5)
737+--     (X →ₜ Aexp.eval st (aexp { X + 1 }) ; st),
738+
739+-- which simplifies to
740+
741+--   fun st =>
742+--     (X →ₜ Aexp.eval st (aexp { X + 1 }) ; st)[X] ≤ 5
743+
744+-- and further simplifies to
745+
746+--   fun st =>
747+--     (Aexp.eval st (aexp { X + 1 })) ≤ 5.
748+
749+-- That is, `P'` is the assertion that `X + 1` is at most `5`.
750+
751+-- We can demonstrate formally that we have captured intuitive meaning of
752+-- "assertion subsitution" by proving some example logical equivalences:
753+
754+namespace ExampleAssertionSub
755+example :
756+    {{ (X ≤ 5) }} [X ↦ 3] <<->> {{ 3 ≤ 5 }} := by
757+  constructor <;> (unfold AssertImplies Assertion.sub; intro st h; exact h)
758+
759+example :
760+    {{ (X ≤ 5) }} [X ↦ X + 1] <<->> {{ (X + 1) ≤ 5 }} := by
761+  constructor <;> (unfold AssertImplies Assertion.sub; intro st h; exact h)
762+
763+end ExampleAssertionSub

445--- ## Hoare Triples, Informally
446-
447--- A *Hoare triple* is a claim about the state before and after executing a
448--- command. A commond notation for Hoare triples, and the one we use in this
449--- book, is
450-
451---   {{P}} c {{Q}}
452-
453--- meaning:
454-
455--- - If command `c` begins execution in a state satisfying assertion `P`,
456--- - and if `c` eventually terminates in some final state,
457--- - then that final state will satisfy the assertion `Q`.
458-
459--- Assertion `P` is called the *precondition* of the triple, and `Q` is the
460--- *postcondition*.
461-
462--- For example,
463-
464--- - The Hoare triple
465-
466---   {{X = 0}} X := X + 1 {{X = 1}}
467-
468--- states that command `X := X + 1` will transform a state in which `X = 0` to
469--- a state in which `X = 1`.
470-
471--- - On the other hand,
472-
473---   ∀ m, {{X = m}} X := X + 1 {{X = m + 1}}
474-
475--- is a *proposition* stating that the Hoare triple
476--- `{{X = m}} X :=
477--- X + 1 {{X = m + 1}}` is valid for any choice of `m`. Note
478--- that `m` in the two assertions is a reference to the *Lean* variable `m`,
479--- which is bound outside the Hoare triple.
480-
481--- _Quiz:_
482-
483--- Paraphrase the following in English.
484-
485---   1) {{True}} c {{X = 5}}
486-
487---   2) ∀ m, {{X = m}} c {{X = m + 5}}
488-
489---   3) {{X ≤ Y}} c {{Y ≤ X}}
490-
491---   4) {{True}} c {{False}}
492-
493---   5) ∀ m,
494---        {{X = m}}
495---        c
496---        {{Y = real_fact m}}
497-
498---   6) ∀ m,
499---        {{X = m}}
500---        c
501---        {{(Z * Z) ≤ m ∧ ¬ ((Z + 1) * (Z + 1) ≤ m)}}

625--- ## Hoare Triples, Formally
626-
627--- We formalize valid Hoare triples in Lean as follows:
628-
629-open scoped HasEval
630-
631-def ValidHoareTriple
632-    (P : Assertion) (c : Com) (Q : Assertion) : Prop :=
633-  ∀ {st st' : State},
634-    (st =[ c ]=> st') →
635-    P st →
636-    Q st'
637-
638--- Notation for Hoare triples. The command between the two assertions is
639--- parsed with the same grammar as the `imp { … }` notation, so a command that
640--- is a Lean variable (rather than concrete syntax) is spliced in with `~c`,
641--- just as in the `st =[ c ]=> st'` notation.
642-
643-class HasTriple (Com : Type) where
644-  Triple : Assertion → Com → Assertion → Prop
645-
646-namespace HasTriple
647-
648-/-- Hoare triple: `{{ P }} c {{ Q }}` -/
649-scoped notation:lead "{{" P "}} " c:lead " {{" Q "}}" => Triple ({{ P }}) c ({{ Q }})
650-
651-/-- Hoare triple with `imp_com` command syntax -/
652-scoped syntax:lead (priority := high) "{{" term "}} " imp_com:lead " {{" term "}}" : term
653-scoped macro_rules
654-  | `({{ $P }} $c:imp_com {{ $Q }}) =>
655-      ``(HasTriple.Triple ({{ $P }}) (imp { $c }) ({{ $Q }}))
656-end HasTriple
657-
658-instance : HasTriple Com where
659-  Triple := ValidHoareTriple
660-
661-open scoped HasTriple
662-
663-theorem validHoareTriple_def {P : Assertion} {c : Com} {Q : Assertion} :
664-    {{ P }} ~c {{ Q }} ↔ ∀ {st st' : State},
665-      (st =[ c ]=> st') →
666-      P st →
667-      Q st' := by rfl
668-
669-attribute [irreducible] ValidHoareTriple

712--- ## Proof Rules
713-
714--- The goal of Hoare logic is to provide a *compositional* method for proving
715--- the validity of specific Hoare triples. That is, we want the structure of a
716--- program's correctness proof to mirror the structure of the program itself.
717--- To this end, in the sections below, we'll introduce a rule for reasoning
718--- about each of the different syntactic forms of commands in Imp -- one for
719--- assignment, one for sequencing, one for conditionals, etc. -- plus a couple
720--- of "structural" rules for gluing things together. We will then be able to
721--- prove programs correct using these proof rules, without ever unfolding the
722--- definition of `ValidHoareTriple`.
723-
724--- ### Skip
725-
726--- Since `skip` doesn't change the state, it preserves any assertion `P`:
727-
728---   --------------------  (hoare_skip)
729---   {{ P }} skip {{ P }}
730-
731-theorem hoare_skip {P : Assertion} :
732-    {{ P }} skip {{ P }} := by
733-  rw [validHoareTriple_def]
734-  intro st st' h hpre
735-  inversion h
736-  exact hpre
737-
738--- ### Sequencing
739-
740--- If command `c1` takes any state where `P` holds to a state where `Q` holds,
741--- and if `c2` takes any state where `Q` holds to one where `R` holds, then
742--- doing `c1` followed by `c2` will take any state where `P` holds to one
743--- where `R` holds:
744-
745---    {{ P }} c1 {{ Q }}
746---    {{ Q }} c2 {{ R }}
747---   ----------------------  (hoare_seq)
748---   {{ P }} c1; c2 {{ R }}
749-
750-theorem hoare_seq {P Q R : Assertion} {c1 c2 : Com}
751-    (h1 : {{ Q }} ~c2 {{ R }}) (h2 : {{ P }} ~c1 {{ Q }}) :
752-    {{ P }} ~c1; ~c2 {{ R }} := by
753-  rw [validHoareTriple_def]
754-  intro st st' h hpre
755-  inversion h with
756-  | seq st'' hc1 hc2 =>
757-    rw [validHoareTriple_def] at h1 h2
758-    exact h1 hc2 (h2 hc1 hpre)
759-
760--- Note that, in the formal rule `hoare_seq`, the premises are given in
761--- backwards order (`c2` before `c1`). This matches the natural flow of
762--- information in many of the situations where we'll use the rule, since the
763--- natural way to construct a Hoare-logic proof is to begin at the end of the
764--- program (with the final postcondition) and push postconditions backwards
765--- through commands until we reach the beginning.
766-
767--- ### Assignment
768-
769--- The rule for assignment is the most fundamental of the Hoare logic proof
770--- rules. Here's how it works.
771-
772--- Consider this incomplete Hoare triple:
773-
774---   {{ ??? }}  X := Y  {{ X = 1 }}
775-
776--- We want to assign `Y` to `X` and finish in a state where `X` is `1`. What
777--- could the precondition be?
778-
779--- One possibility is `Y = 1`, because if `Y` is already `1` then assigning it
780--- to `X` causes `X` to be `1`. That leads to a valid Hoare triple:
781-
782---   {{ Y = 1 }}  X := Y  {{ X = 1 }}
783-
784--- It may seem as though coming up with that precondition must have taken some
785--- clever thought. But there is a mechanical way we could have done it: if we
786--- take the postcondition `X = 1` and in it replace `X` with `Y`---that is,
787--- replace the left-hand side of the assignment statement with the right-hand
788--- side---we get the precondition, `Y = 1`.
789-
790--- That same idea works in more complicated cases. For example:
791-
792---   {{ ??? }}  X := X + Y  {{ X = 1 }}
793-
794--- If we replace the `X` in `X = 1` with `X + Y`, we get `X + Y = 1`. That
795--- again leads to a valid Hoare triple:
796-
797---   {{ X + Y = 1 }}  X := X + Y  {{ X = 1 }}
798-
799--- Why does this technique work? The postcondition identifies some property
800--- `P` that we want to hold of the variable `X` being assigned. In this case,
801--- `P` is "equals `1`". To complete the triple and make it valid, we need to
802--- identify a precondition that guarantees that property will hold of `X`.
803--- Such a precondition must ensure that the same property holds of *whatever
804--- is being assigned to* `X`. So, in the example, we need "equals `1`" to hold
805--- of `X + Y`. That's exactly what the technique guarantees.
806-
807--- In general, the postcondition could be some arbitrary assertion `Q`, and
808--- the right-hand side of the assignment could be some arbitrary arithmetic
809--- expression `a`:
810-
811---   {{ ??? }}  X := a  {{ Q }}
812-
813--- The precondition would then be `Q`, but with any occurrences of `X` in it
814--- replaced by `a`.
815-
816--- Let's introduce a notation for this idea of replacing occurrences: Define
817--- `Q \[X ↦ a`] to mean "`Q` where `a` is substituted in place of `X`".
818-
819--- This yields the Hoare logic rule for assignment:
820-
821---   {{ Q [X ↦ a] }}  X := a  {{ Q }}
822-
823--- One way of reading this rule is: If you want statement `X := a` to
824--- terminate in a state that satisfies assertion `Q`, then it suffices to
825--- start in a state that also satisfies `Q`, except where `a` is substituted
826--- for every occurrence of `X`.
827-
828--- To many people, this rule seems "backwards" at first, because it proceeds
829--- from the postcondition to the precondition. Actually it makes good sense to
830--- go in this direction: the postcondition is often what is more important,
831--- because it characterizes what will be true after running the code.
832-
833--- Nonetheless, it's also possible to formulate a "forward" assignment rule.
834--- We'll do that later in some exercises.
835-
836--- Here are some valid instances of the assignment rule:
837-
838---   {{ (X ≤ 5) [X ↦ X + 1] }}         (that is, X + 1 ≤ 5)
839---     X := X + 1
840---   {{ X ≤ 5 }}
841-
842---   {{ (X = 3) [X ↦ 3] }}              (that is, 3 = 3)
843---     X := 3
844---   {{ X = 3 }}
845-
846---   {{ (0 ≤ X ∧ X ≤ 5) [X ↦ 3] }}.  (that is, 0 ≤ 3 ∧ 3 ≤ 5)
847---     X := 3
848---   {{ 0 ≤ X ∧ X ≤ 5 }}
849-
850--- To formalize the rule, we must first formalize the idea of "substituting an
851--- expression for an Imp variable in an assertion", which we refer to as
852--- assertion substitution, or `Assertion.subst`.
853-
854--- Intuitively, given a proposition `P`, a variable `X`, and an arithmetic
855--- expression `a`, we want to derive another proposition `P'` that is just the
856--- same as `P` except that `P'` should mention `a` wherever `P` mentions `X`.
857-
858--- This operation is related to the idea of substituting Imp expressions for
859--- Imp variables that we saw in *Equiv* (`subst_aexp` and friends). The
860--- difference is that, here, `P` is an arbitrary Lean assertion, so we can't
861--- directly "edit" its text.
862-
863--- However, we can achieve the same effect by evaluating `P` in an updated
864--- state, defined as follows:
865-
866-def Assertion.subst (x : Ident) (a : Aexp) (P : Assertion) : Assertion :=
867-  fun (st : State) => P (x →ₜ a.eval st ; st)
868-
869-namespace Assertion
870-
871-/-- Assertion substitution, written inside the braces: `{{ (P) [X ↦ a] }}`.
872-The substituted assertion is re-read with the same notation, so Imp
873-variables in it mean state lookups as usual; a named assertion is passed
874-through directly. -/
875-scoped syntax:max term:arg " [" ident " ↦ " imp_aexp "]" : term
876-
877-macro_rules
878-  | `(assn($st; $P [$x ↦ $a:imp_aexp])) =>
879-    match P with
880-    | `($_:ident) => ``(Assertion.subst $x (aexp { $a }) $P $st)
881-    | _ => ``(Assertion.subst $x (aexp { $a }) ({{ $P }}) $st)
882-
883-theorem subst_def {x : Ident} {a : Aexp} {P : Assertion} :
884-    Assertion.subst x a P = fun (st : State) => P (x →ₜ a.eval st ; st) := by rfl
885-
886-@[simp]
887-theorem subst_apply {x : Ident} {a : Aexp} {P : Assertion} {st : State} :
888-    Assertion.subst x a P st ↔ P (x →ₜ a.eval st ; st) := by rfl
889-
890-end Assertion
891-

5+-- # Hoare2: Hoare Logic, Part II
6+
7+open scoped Assertion ValidHoareTriple
8+
9+-- _Quiz:_
10+
11+-- On a piece of paper (or whatever), write down a Hoare-triple specification
12+-- for the following program:
13+
14+--   X := 2;
15+--   Y := X + X
16+
17+-- _Quiz:_
18+
19+-- Write down a (useful) specification for the following program:
20+
21+--   X := X + 1; Y := X + 1
22+
23+-- _Quiz:_
24+
25+-- Write down a (useful) specification for the following program:
26+
27+--   if X <= Y then
28+--     skip
29+--   else
30+--     Z := X;
31+--     X := Y;
32+--     Y := Z
33+--   end
34+
35+-- _Quiz:_
36+
37+-- Write down a (useful) specification for the following program:
38+
39+--   X := m;
40+--   Y := X + X
41+
42+-- _Quiz:_
43+
44+-- Write down a (useful) specification for the following program:
45+
46+--   X := m;
47+--   Z := 0;
48+--   while X <> 0 do
49+--     X := X - 2;
50+--     Z := Z + 1
51+--   end
52+
53+-- ## Decorated Programs
54+
55+-- The beauty of Hoare Logic is that it is *syntax directed*: the structure of
56+-- proofs exactly follows the structure of programs.
57+
58+-- We can record the essential ideas of a Hoare-logic proof — omitting
59+-- low-level calculational details — by "decorating" a program with
60+-- appropriate assertions on each of its commands.
61+
62+-- Such a *decorated program* carries within itself an argument for its own
63+-- correctness.
64+
65+-- For example, consider the program:
66+
67+--   X := m;
68+--   Z := p;
69+--   while X <> 0 do
70+--     Z := Z - 1;
71+--     X := X - 1
72+--   end
73+
74+-- Here is one possible specification for this program, in the form of a Hoare
75+-- triple:
76+
77+--   {{ True }}
78+--   X := m;
79+--   Z := p;
80+--   while X <> 0 do
81+--     Z := Z - 1;
82+--     X := X - 1
83+--   end
84+--   {{ Z = p - m }}
85+
86+-- (Note the *parameters* `m` and `p`, which stand for fixed-but-arbitrary
87+-- numbers. Formally, they are simply Lean variables of type `Nat`.)
88+
89+-- Here is a decorated version of this program, embodying a proof of this
90+-- specification:
91+
92+--   {{ True }} ->>
93+--   {{ m = m }}
94+--     X := m
95+--                        {{ X = m }} ->>
96+--                        {{ X = m /\ p = p }};
97+--     Z := p;
98+--                        {{ X = m /\ Z = p }} ->>
99+--                        {{ Z - X = p - m }}
100+--     while X <> 0 do
101+--                        {{ Z - X = p - m /\ X <> 0 }} ->>
102+--                        {{ (Z - 1) - (X - 1) = p - m }}
103+--       Z := Z - 1
104+--                        {{ Z - (X - 1) = p - m }};
105+--       X := X - 1
106+--                        {{ Z - X = p - m }}
107+--     end
108+--   {{ Z - X = p - m /\ ~ (X <> 0) }} ->>
109+--   {{ Z = p - m }}
110+
111+-- Concretely, a decorated program consists of the program's text interleaved
112+-- with assertions (sometimes multiple assertions separated by ->>).
113+
114+-- A decorated program can be viewed as a compact representation of a proof in
115+-- Hoare Logic: the assertions surrounding each command specify the Hoare
116+-- triple to be proved for that part of the program using one of the Hoare
117+-- Logic rules, and the structure of the program itself shows how to assemble
118+-- all these individual steps into a proof for the whole program.
119+
120+-- Our goal is to verify such decorated programs "mostly automatically." But,
121+-- before we can verify anything, we need to be able to *find* a proof for a
122+-- given specification, and for this we need to discover the right assertions.
123+-- This can be done in an almost mechanical way, with the exception of finding
124+-- loop invariants. In the remainder of this section, we explain in detail how
125+-- to construct decorations for several short programs, all of which are loop
126+-- free or have simple loop invariants. We'll return to finding more
127+-- interesting loop invariants later in the chapter.
128+
129+-- ### Example: Swapping
130+
131+-- Consider the following program, which swaps the values of two variables
132+-- using addition and subtraction, instead of by assigning to a temporary
133+-- variable.
134+
135+--   X := X + Y;
136+--   Y := X - Y;
137+--   X := X - Y
138+
139+-- We can give a proof, in the form of decorations, that this program is
140+-- correct — i.e., it really swaps `X` and `Y` — as follows.
141+
142+--   (1)    {{ X = m /\ Y = n }} ->>
143+--   (2)    {{ (X + Y) - ((X + Y) - Y) = n /\ (X + Y) - Y = m }}
144+--            X := X + Y
145+--   (3)                     {{ X - (X - Y) = n /\ X - Y = m }};
146+--            Y := X - Y
147+--   (4)                     {{ X - Y = n /\ Y = m }};
148+--            X := X - Y
149+--   (5)    {{ X = n /\ Y = m }}
150+
151+-- The decorations can be constructed as follows:
152+
153+-- - We begin with the undecorated program (the unnumbered lines).
154+
155+-- - We add the specification — i.e., the outer precondition (1) and
156+--   postcondition (5). In the precondition, we use parameters `m` and `n` to
157+--   remember the initial values of variables `X` and `Y` so that we can refer
158+--   to them in the postcondition (5).
159+
160+-- - We work backwards, mechanically, starting from (5) and proceeding until we
161+--   get to (2). At each step, we obtain the precondition of the assignment from
162+--   its postcondition by substituting the assigned variable with the
163+--   right-hand-side of the assignment. For instance, we obtain (4) by
164+--   substituting `X` with `X - Y` in (5), and we obtain (3) by substituting `Y`
165+--   with `X - Y` in (4).
166+
167+-- - Finally, we verify that (1) logically implies (2) — i.e., that the step
168+--   from (1) to (2) is a valid use of the law of consequence — by doing a bit
169+--   of high-school algebra.
170+
171+-- ### Example: Simple Conditionals
172+
173+-- Here is a simple decorated program using conditionals:
174+
175+--   (1)   {{ True }}
176+--           if X <= Y then
177+--   (2)                    {{ True /\ X <= Y }} ->>
178+--   (3)                    {{ (Y - X) + X = Y \/ (Y - X) + Y = X }}
179+--             Z := Y - X
180+--   (4)                    {{ Z + X = Y \/ Z + Y = X }}
181+--           else
182+--   (5)                    {{ True /\ ~(X <= Y) }} ->>
183+--   (6)                    {{ (X - Y) + X = Y \/ (X - Y) + Y = X }}
184+--             Z := X - Y
185+--   (7)                    {{ Z + X = Y \/ Z + Y = X }}
186+--           end
187+--   (8)   {{ Z + X = Y \/ Z + Y = X }}
188+
189+-- These decorations can be constructed as follows:
190+
191+-- - We start with the outer precondition (1) and postcondition (8).
192+
193+-- - Following the format dictated by the `hoare_if` rule, we copy the
194+--   postcondition (8) to (4) and (7). We conjoin the precondition (1) with the
195+--   guard of the conditional to obtain (2). We conjoin (1) with the negated
196+--   guard of the conditional to obtain (5).
197+
198+-- - In order to use the assignment rule and obtain (3), we substitute `Z` by
199+--   `Y - X` in (4). To obtain (6) we substitute `Z` by `X - Y` in (7).
200+
201+-- - Finally, we verify that (2) implies (3) and (5) implies (6). Both of these
202+--   implications crucially depend on the ordering of `X` and `Y` obtained from
203+--   the guard. For instance, knowing that `X <= Y` ensures that subtracting `X`
204+--   from `Y` and then adding back `X` produces `Y`, as required by the first
205+--   disjunct of (3). Similarly, knowing that `~ (X <= Y)` ensures that
206+--   subtracting `Y` from `X` and then adding back `Y` produces `X`, as needed
207+--   by the second disjunct of (6). Note that `n - m + m = n` does *not* hold
208+--   for arbitrary natural numbers `n` and `m` (for example, [3 - 5 + 5 = 5]).
209+
210+-- ### Exercise (2 stars): if_minus_plus_reloaded (manually graded) ⭐⭐
211+
212+-- N.b.: Although this exercise is marked optional, it is an excellent warm-up
213+-- for the (non-optional) `if_minus_plus_correct` exercise below!
214+
215+-- Fill in valid decorations for the following program:
216+
217+--   {{ True }}
218+--     if X <= Y then
219+--               {{                         }} ->>
220+--               {{                         }}
221+--       Z := Y - X
222+--               {{                         }}
223+--     else
224+--               {{                         }} ->>
225+--               {{                         }}
226+--       Y := X + Z
227+--               {{                         }}
228+--     end
229+--   {{ Y = X + Z }}
230+
231+-- Briefly justify each use of `->>`.
232+
233+-- ### Example: Reduce to Zero
234+
235+-- Here is a `while` loop that is so simple that `True` suffices as a loop
236+-- invariant.
237+
238+--   (1)    {{ True }}
239+--            while X <> 0 do
240+--   (2)                  {{ True /\ X <> 0 }} ->>
241+--   (3)                  {{ True }}
242+--              X := X - 1
243+--   (4)                  {{ True }}
244+--            end
245+--   (5)    {{ True /\ ~(X <> 0) }} ->>
246+--   (6)    {{ X = 0 }}
247+
248+-- The decorations can be constructed as follows:
249+
250+-- - Start with the outer precondition (1) and postcondition (6).
251+
252+-- - Following the format dictated by the `hoare_while` rule, we copy (1) to
253+--   (4). We conjoin (1) with the guard to obtain (2). We also conjoin (1) with
254+--   the negation of the guard to obtain (5).
255+
256+-- - Because the final postcondition (6) does not syntactically match (5), we
257+--   add an implication between them.
258+
259+-- - Using the assignment rule with assertion (4), we trivially substitute and
260+--   obtain assertion (3).
261+
262+-- - We add the implication between (2) and (3).
263+
264+-- Finally we check that the implications do hold; both are trivial.
265+
266+-- ### Example: Division
267+
268+-- Let's do one more example of simple reasoning about a loop.
269+
270+-- The following Imp program calculates the integer quotient and remainder of
271+-- parameters `m` and `n`.
272+
273+--   X := m;
274+--   Y := 0;
275+--   while n <= X do
276+--     X := X - n;
277+--     Y := Y + 1
278+--   end;
279+
280+-- If we replace `m` and `n` by concrete numbers and execute the program, it
281+-- will terminate with the variable `X` set to the remainder when `m` is
282+-- divided by `n` and `Y` set to the quotient.
283+
284+-- In order to give a specification to this program we need to remember that
285+-- dividing `m` by `n` produces a remainder `X` and a quotient `Y` such that
286+-- `n * Y + X = m /\ X < n`.
287+
288+-- It turns out that we get lucky with this program and don't have to think
289+-- very hard about the loop invariant: the loop invariant is just the first
290+-- conjunct, `n * Y + X = m`, and we can use this to decorate the program.
291+
292+--    (1)  {{ True }} ->>
293+--    (2)  {{ n * 0 + m = m }}
294+--           X := m;
295+--    (3)                     {{ n * 0 + X = m }}
296+--           Y := 0;
297+--    (4)                     {{ n * Y + X = m }}
298+--           while n <= X do
299+--    (5)                     {{ n * Y + X = m /\ n <= X }} ->>
300+--    (6)                     {{ n * (Y + 1) + (X - n) = m }}
301+--             X := X - n;
302+--    (7)                     {{ n * (Y + 1) + X = m }}
303+--             Y := Y + 1
304+--    (8)                     {{ n * Y + X = m }}
305+--           end
306+--    (9)  {{ n * Y + X = m /\ ~ (n <= X) }} ->>
307+--   (10)  {{ n * Y + X = m /\ X < n }}
308+
309+-- Assertions (4), (5), (8), and (9) are derived mechanically from the loop
310+-- invariant and the loop's guard. Assertions (8), (7), and (6) are derived
311+-- using the assignment rule going backwards from (8) to (6). Assertions (4),
312+-- (3), and (2) are again backwards applications of the assignment rule.
313+
314+-- Now that we've decorated the program it only remains to check that the uses
315+-- of the consequence rule are correct — i.e., that (1) implies (2), that (5)
316+-- implies (6), and that (9) implies (10). This is indeed the case:
317+
318+-- - (1) ->> (2): trivial, by algebra.
319+
320+-- - (5) ->> (6): because `n <= X`, we are guaranteed that the subtraction in
321+--   (6) does not get zero-truncated. We can therefore rewrite (6) as
322+--   `n * Y + n + X - n` and cancel the `n`s, which results in the left conjunct
323+--   of (5).
324+
325+-- - (9) ->> (10): if `~ (n <= X)` then `X < n`. That's straightforward from
326+--   high-school algebra. So, we have a valid decorated program.
327+
328+-- ### From Decorated Programs to Formal Proofs
329+
330+-- From an informal proof in the form of a decorated program, it is "easy in
331+-- principle" to read off a formal proof using the Lean theorems corresponding
332+-- to the Hoare Logic rules, but these proofs can be a bit long and fiddly.
333+
334+-- Note that we do *not* unfold the definition of `ValidHoareTriple` anywhere
335+-- in this proof: the point of the game we're playing now is to use the Hoare
336+-- rules as a self-contained logic for reasoning about programs.
337+
338+-- For example...
339+
340+def reduceToZero : Com :=
341+  imp {
342+    while (X ≠ 0) {
343+      X := X - 1;
344+    }
345+  }
346+
347+theorem reduce_to_zero_correct' :
348+    {{ True }} ~reduceToZero {{ X = 0 }} := by
349+  -- First put the postcondition into the form expected by
350+  -- the while rule.
351+  sorry
352+
353+-- In Hoare we introduced a series of tactics named `assertion_auto` to
354+-- automate proofs involving assertions.
355+
356+-- The following declaration introduces a more sophisticated tactic that will
357+-- help with proving assertions throughout the rest of this chapter. You don't
358+-- need to understand the details, but briefly: it introduces the available
359+-- hypotheses, simplifies assertions, maps, and arithmetic expressions, and
360+-- then asks `lia` to solve linear arithmetic goals. What's left after
361+-- `verify_assertion` does its work should be just the "interesting parts" of
362+-- the proof (which, if we're lucky, might be nothing at all!).
363+
364+macro "verify_assertion" : tactic =>
365+  `(tactic| assertion_auto')
366+
367+-- This makes it pretty easy to verify `reduce_to_zero`:
368+
369+theorem reduce_to_zero_correct''' :
370+    {{ True }} ~reduceToZero {{ X = 0 }} := by
371+  sorry
372+
373+-- This example shows that it is conceptually straightforward to read off the
374+-- main elements of a formal proof from a decorated program. Indeed, the
375+-- process is so straightforward that it can be automated, as we will see
376+-- next.
377+
378+-- ## Formal Decorated Programs
379+
380+-- Our informal conventions for decorated programs amount to a way of
381+-- "displaying" Hoare triples, in which commands are annotated with enough
382+-- embedded assertions that checking the validity of a triple is reduced to
383+-- simple logical and algebraic calculations showing that some assertions
384+-- imply others.
385+
386+-- In this section, we show that this presentation style can be made
387+-- completely formal — and indeed that checking the validity of decorated
388+-- programs can be largely automated.
389+
390+-- ### Syntax
391+
392+-- The first thing we need to do is to formalize a variant of the syntax of
393+-- Imp commands that includes embedded assertions, which we'll call
394+-- "decorations." We call the new commands *decorated commands*, or `dcom`s.
395+
396+-- The choice of exactly where to put assertions in the definition of `dcom`
397+-- is a bit subtle. The simplest thing to do would be to annotate every `dcom`
398+-- with a precondition and postcondition — something like this...
399+
400+namespace DComFirstTry
401+
402+inductive DCom where
403+  | skip (pre : Assertion)
404+  | seq (pre : Assertion) (first : DCom)
405+      (middle : Assertion)
406+      (second : DCom) (post : Assertion)
407+  | asgn (x : Ident) (a : Aexp) (post : Assertion)
408+  | cond (pre : Assertion) (b : Bexp)
409+      (thenPre : Assertion) (thenBranch : DCom)
410+      (elsePre : Assertion) (elseBranch : DCom)
411+      (post : Assertion)
412+  | whileDo (pre : Assertion) (b : Bexp)
413+      (bodyPre : Assertion) (body : DCom)
414+      (bodyPost : Assertion) (post : Assertion)
415+  | strengthenPre (pre : Assertion) (body : DCom)
416+  | weakenPost (body : DCom) (post : Assertion)
417+
418+end DComFirstTry
419+
420+-- But this would result in *very* verbose decorated programs with a lot of
421+-- repeated annotations: a simple program like `skip;skip` would be decorated
422+-- like this,
423+
424+--   {{P}} ({{P}} skip {{P}}) ; ({{P}} skip {{P}}) {{P}}
425+
426+-- with pre- and post-conditions around each `skip`, plus identical pre- and
427+-- post-conditions on the semicolon!
428+
429+-- In other words, we don't want both preconditions and postconditions on each
430+-- command, because a sequence of two commands would contain redundant
431+-- decorations — the postcondition of the first likely being the same as the
432+-- precondition of the second.
433+
434+-- Instead, our formal syntax of decorated commands will omit preconditions
435+-- whenever possible and embed just postconditions.
436+
437+-- - The `skip` command, for example, is decorated only with its postcondition
438+
439+--   skip {{ Q }}
440+
441+-- on the assumption that the precondition will be provided by somebody else.
442+
443+-- We carry the same assumption through the other syntactic forms: each
444+-- decorated command is assumed to carry its own postcondition within itself
445+-- but take its precondition from its context in which it is used.
446+
447+-- - Sequences `d1 ; d2` need no additional decorations.
448+
449+-- Why?
450+
451+-- Because inside `d2` there will be a postcondition, which also serves as the
452+-- postcondition of `d1;d2`.
453+
454+-- Similarly, inside `d1` there will also be a postcondition, which
455+-- additionally serves as the *precondition* for `d2`.
456+
457+-- - An assignment `X := a` is decorated only with its postcondition:
458+
459+--   X := a {{ Q }}
460+
461+-- - A conditional `if b then d1 else d2` is decorated with a postcondition for
462+--   the entire statement, as well as preconditions for each branch:
463+
464+--   if b then {{ P1 }} d1 else {{ P2 }} d2 end {{ Q }}
465+
466+-- - A loop `while b do d end` is decorated with its final postcondition plus a
467+--   precondition for the body:
468+
469+--   while b do {{ P }} d end {{ Q }}
470+
471+-- The postcondition embedded in `d` serves as the loop invariant.
472+
473+-- - Implications `->>` can be added as decorations either for a precondition...
474+
475+--   ->> {{ P }} d
476+
477+-- ...or for a postcondition:
478+
479+--   d ->> {{ Q }}
480+
481+-- The former is waiting for another precondition to be supplied by the
482+-- context; the latter relies on the postcondition already embedded in `d`.
483+
484+-- Putting this all together gives us the formal syntax of decorated commands:
485+
486+inductive DCom where
487+  | skip (post : Assertion)
488+  | seq (first second : DCom)
489+  | asgn (x : Ident) (a : Aexp) (post : Assertion)
490+  | cond (b : Bexp)
491+      (thenPre : Assertion) (thenBranch : DCom)
492+      (elsePre : Assertion) (elseBranch : DCom)
493+      (post : Assertion)
494+  | whileDo (b : Bexp) (bodyPre : Assertion) (body : DCom)
495+      (post : Assertion)
496+  | pre (pre : Assertion) (body : DCom)
497+  | post (body : DCom) (post : Assertion)
498+
499+-- Lean keeps decorated-command notation in its own syntax category, `dcom`,
500+-- so it can coexist with the ordinary Imp command syntax.
501+
502+-- THESE DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED: Notation encoding: decorated commands
503+
504+declare_syntax_cat dcom
505+
506+syntax:max "(" dcom ")" : dcom
507+syntax:max "skip" " {{" term "}}" : dcom
508+syntax:max ident " := " imp_aexp " {{" term "}}" : dcom
509+syntax:20 dcom:21 ";" ppLine dcom:20 : dcom
510+syntax:max "if " "(" imp_bexp ")" ppHardSpace "then" ppLine
511+  "{{" term "}}" ppLine dcom ppLine
512+  "else" ppLine "{{" term "}}" ppLine dcom ppLine
513+  "end" ppLine "{{" term "}}" : dcom
514+syntax:max "while " "(" imp_bexp ")" ppHardSpace "do" ppLine
515+  "{{" term "}}" ppLine dcom ppLine
516+  "end" ppLine "{{" term "}}" : dcom
517+syntax:5 "->>" " {{" term "}}" ppLine dcom:0 : dcom
518+syntax:5 dcom:6 ppLine "->>" " {{" term "}}" : dcom
519+
520+syntax:min "dcom" ppHardSpace "{" ppLine dcom
521+  ppDedent(ppLine "}") : term
522+
523+macro_rules
524+  | `(dcom { ($body:dcom) }) =>
525+      `(dcom { $body })
526+  | `(dcom { skip {{ $q }} }) =>
527+      `(DCom.skip ({{ $q }}))
528+  | `(dcom { $x:ident := $a:imp_aexp {{ $q }} }) =>
529+      `(DCom.asgn $x (aexp { $a }) ({{ $q }}))
530+  | `(dcom { $d1:dcom; $d2:dcom }) =>
531+      `(DCom.seq (dcom { $d1 }) (dcom { $d2 }))
532+  | `(dcom {
533+        if ($b:imp_bexp) then
534+          {{ $p1 }}
535+          $d1:dcom
536+        else
537+          {{ $p2 }}
538+          $d2:dcom
539+        end
540+          {{ $q }}
541+      }) =>
542+      `(DCom.cond (bexp { $b })
543+        ({{ $p1 }}) (dcom { $d1 })
544+        ({{ $p2 }}) (dcom { $d2 })
545+        ({{ $q }}))
546+  | `(dcom {
547+        while ($b:imp_bexp) do
548+          {{ $p }}
549+          $body:dcom
550+        end
551+          {{ $q }}
552+      }) =>
553+      `(DCom.whileDo (bexp { $b }) ({{ $p }})
554+        (dcom { $body }) ({{ $q }}))
555+  | `(dcom { ->> {{ $p }} $body:dcom }) =>
556+      `(DCom.pre ({{ $p }}) (dcom { $body }))
557+  | `(dcom { $body:dcom ->> {{ $q }} }) =>
558+      `(DCom.post (dcom { $body }) ({{ $q }}))
559+
560+-- END DETAILS
561+
562+-- To provide the initial precondition that goes at the very top of a
563+-- decorated program, we introduce a new type `decorated`:
564+
565+structure Decorated where
566+  pre : Assertion
567+  body : DCom
568+
569+example : DCom :=
570+  .skip {{ True }}
571+
572+example : DCom :=
573+  .whileDo (bexp {true}) {{ True }}
574+    (.skip {{ True }}) {{ True }}
575+
576+-- To inspect the fully elaborated term behind this notation, put
577+-- `set_option pp.all true in` before a `#check` or `#print` command.
578+
579+-- The formal definitions can use either constructors directly or the
580+-- decorated-command notation introduced above.
581+
582+-- An example `decorated` program that decrements `X` to `0`:
583+
584+def decWhile : Decorated where
585+  pre := ({{ True }})
586+  body := dcom {
587+    while (X ≠ 0) do
588+      {{ True ∧ ¬ X = 0 }}
589+      X := X - 1 {{ True }}
590+    end
591+      {{ True ∧ X = 0 }}
592+    ->> {{ X = 0 }}
593+  }
594+
595+-- It is easy to go from a `dcom` to a `com` by erasing all annotations.
596+
597+def DCom.erase (d : DCom) : Com :=
598+  match d with
599+  | .skip _ => .skip
600+  | .seq d1 d2 => .seq d1.erase d2.erase
601+  | .asgn x a _ => .asgn x a
602+  | .cond b _ d1 _ d2 _ => .cond b d1.erase d2.erase
603+  | .whileDo b _ body _ => .whileDo b body.erase
604+  | .pre _ body => body.erase
605+  | .post body _ => body.erase
606+
607+def Decorated.erase (dec : Decorated) : Com :=
608+  dec.body.erase
609+
610+example :
611+    decWhile.erase =
612+      (imp {
613+        while (X ≠ 0) {
614+          X := X - 1;
615+        }
616+      }) := by
617+  rfl
618+
619+-- It is also straightforward to extract the precondition and postcondition
620+-- from a decorated program.
621+
622+def Decorated.precondition (dec : Decorated) : Assertion :=
623+  dec.pre
624+
625+def DCom.postcondition (d : DCom) : Assertion :=
626+  match d with
627+  | .skip q => q
628+  | .seq _ d2 => d2.postcondition
629+  | .asgn _ _ q => q
630+  | .cond _ _ _ _ _ q => q
631+  | .whileDo _ _ _ q => q
632+  | .pre _ body => body.postcondition
633+  | .post _ q => q
634+
635+def Decorated.postcondition (dec : Decorated) : Assertion :=
636+  dec.body.postcondition
637+
638+example : decWhile.precondition = {{ True }} := by
639+  funext st
640+  rfl
641+
642+example : decWhile.postcondition = {{ X = 0 }} := by
643+  funext st
644+  rfl
645+
646+-- We can then express what it means for a decorated program to be correct as
647+-- follows:
648+
649+def Decorated.OuterTripleValid (dec : Decorated) : Prop :=
650+  ValidHoareTriple dec.precondition dec.erase
651+    dec.postcondition
652+
653+-- For example:
654+
655+example :
656+    decWhile.OuterTripleValid =
657+      ValidHoareTriple
658+        {{ True }}
659+        (imp {
660+          while (X ≠ 0) {
661+            X := X - 1;
662+          }
663+        })
664+        {{ X = 0 }} := by
665+  rfl
666+
667+-- The outer Hoare triple of a decorated program is just a `Prop`; thus, to
668+-- show that it is *valid*, we need to produce a proof of this proposition.
669+
670+-- We will do this by extracting "proof obligations" from the decorations
671+-- sprinkled throughout the program.
672+
673+-- These obligations are often called *verification conditions*, because they
674+-- are the facts that must be verified to see that the decorations are locally
675+-- consistent and thus constitute a proof of validity of the outer triple.
676+
677+-- ### Extracting Verification Conditions
678+
679+-- The function `DCom.VerificationConditions` takes a decorated command `d`
680+-- together with a precondition `P` and returns a *proposition* that, if it
681+-- can be proved, implies that the triple
682+
683+--   {{P}} d.erase {{d.postcondition}}
684+
685+-- is valid.
686+
687+-- It does this by walking over `d` and generating a big conjunction that
688+-- includes
689+
690+-- - local consistency checks for each form of command, plus
691+
692+-- - uses of `->>` to bridge the gap between the assertions found inside a
693+--   decorated command and the assertions imposed by the external precondition;
694+--   these uses correspond to applications of the consequence rule.
695+
696+-- *Local consistency* is defined as follows...
697+
698+-- - The decorated command
699+
700+--   skip {{Q}}
701+
702+-- is locally consistent with respect to a precondition `P` if `P ->> Q`.
703+
704+-- - The sequential composition of `d1` and `d2` is locally consistent with
705+--   respect to `P` if `d1` is locally consistent with respect to `P` and `d2`
706+--   is locally consistent with respect to the postcondition of `d1`.
707+
708+-- - An assignment
709+
710+--   X := a {{Q}}
711+
712+-- is locally consistent with respect to a precondition `P` if:
713+
714+--   P ->> Q [X |-> a]
715+
716+-- - A conditional
717+
718+--   if b then {{P1}} d1 else {{P2}} d2 end {{Q}}
719+
720+-- is locally consistent with respect to precondition `P` if
721+
722+-- (1) `P /\ b ->> P1`
723+
724+-- (2) `P /\ ~b ->> P2`
725+
726+-- (3) `d1` is locally consistent with respect to `P1`
727+
728+-- (4) `d2` is locally consistent with respect to `P2`
729+
730+-- (5) `d1.postcondition ->> Q`
731+
732+-- (6) `d2.postcondition ->> Q`
733+
734+-- - A loop
735+
736+--   while b do {{Q}} d end {{R}}
737+
738+-- is locally consistent with respect to precondition `P` if:
739+
740+-- (1) `P ->> d.postcondition`
741+
742+-- (2) `d.postcondition /\ b ->> Q`
743+
744+-- (3) `d.postcondition /\ ~b ->> R`
745+
746+-- (4) `d` is locally consistent with respect to `Q`
747+
748+-- - A command with an extra assertion at the beginning
749+
750+--   ->> {{Q}} d
751+
752+-- is locally consistent with respect to a precondition `P` if:
753+
754+-- (1) `P ->> Q`
755+
756+-- (2) `d` is locally consistent with respect to `Q`
757+
758+-- - A command with an extra assertion at the end
759+
760+--   d ->> {{Q}}
761+
762+-- is locally consistent with respect to a precondition `P` if:
763+
764+-- (1) `d` is locally consistent with respect to `P`
765+
766+-- (2) `d.postcondition ->> Q`
767+
768+-- With all this in mind, we can write a *verification condition generator*
769+-- that takes a decorated command and reads off a proposition saying that all
770+-- its decorations are locally consistent.
771+
772+-- Formally, since a decorated command is "waiting for its precondition" the
773+-- main VC generator takes a `dcom` plus a given precondition as arguments.
774+
775+def DCom.VerificationConditions
776+    (P : Assertion) (d : DCom) : Prop :=
777+  match d with
778+  | .skip Q =>
779+      P ->> Q
780+  | .seq d1 d2 =>
781+      d1.VerificationConditions P ∧
782+      d2.VerificationConditions d1.postcondition
783+  | .asgn x a Q =>
784+      P ->> Q [x ↦ ~a]
785+  | .cond b P1 d1 P2 d2 Q =>
786+      ({{ P ∧ b }} ->> P1) ∧
787+      ({{ P ∧ ¬ b }} ->> P2) ∧
788+      (d1.postcondition ->> Q) ∧
789+      (d2.postcondition ->> Q) ∧
790+      d1.VerificationConditions P1 ∧
791+      d2.VerificationConditions P2
792+  | .whileDo b bodyPre body q =>
793+      -- The body's postcondition is both the loop invariant
794+      -- and the precondition for the first iteration.
795+      (P ->> body.postcondition) ∧
796+      ({{ body.postcondition ∧ b }} ->> bodyPre) ∧
797+      ({{ body.postcondition ∧ ¬ b }} ->> q) ∧
798+      body.VerificationConditions bodyPre
799+  | .pre P' body =>
800+      (P ->> P') ∧ body.VerificationConditions P'
801+  | .post body Q =>
802+      body.VerificationConditions P ∧
803+      (body.postcondition ->> Q)
804+
805+-- The following key theorem states that `DCom.VerificationConditions` does
806+-- its job correctly. Not surprisingly, each of the Hoare Logic rules plays a
807+-- critical role at some point in the proof.
808+
809+theorem verification_correct (d : DCom) (P : Assertion)
810+    (hvc : d.VerificationConditions P) :
811+    ValidHoareTriple P d.erase d.postcondition := by
812+  sorry
813+
814+-- Now that all the pieces are in place, we can define what it means to verify
815+-- an entire program.
816+
817+def Decorated.VerificationConditions
818+    (dec : Decorated) : Prop :=
819+  dec.body.VerificationConditions dec.pre
820+
821+-- And this brings us to the main theorem of this section:
822+
823+theorem verification_conditions_correct (dec : Decorated)
824+    (hvc : dec.VerificationConditions) :
825+    dec.OuterTripleValid := by
826+  exact verification_correct dec.body dec.pre hvc
827+
828+-- ### More Automation
829+
830+-- The propositions generated by `DCom.VerificationConditions` are fairly big
831+-- and contain many conjuncts that are essentially trivial.
832+
833+example : decWhile.VerificationConditions := by
834+  unfold Decorated.VerificationConditions decWhile
835+  simp only [DCom.VerificationConditions,
836+    DCom.postcondition]
837+  sorry
838+
839+-- Fortunately, our `verify_assertion` tactic can generally take care of most
840+-- (or sometimes all) of them.
841+
842+example : decWhile.VerificationConditions := by
843+  sorry
844+
845+-- To automate the overall process of verification, we can use
846+-- `verification_correct` to extract the verification conditions, use
847+-- `verify_assertion` to verify them as much as it can, and finally tidy up
848+-- any remaining bits by hand.
849+
850+macro "verify" : tactic =>
851+  `(tactic|
852+    (apply verification_conditions_correct;
853+     verify_assertion))
854+
855+-- Here's the final, formal proof that `decWhile` is correct.
856+
857+theorem dec_while_correct :
858+    decWhile.OuterTripleValid := by
859+  sorry
860+
861+-- Similarly, here is the formal decorated program for the "swapping by adding
862+-- and subtracting" example that we saw earlier.
863+
864+def swapDec (m n : Nat) : Decorated where
865+  pre := ({{ X = m ∧ Y = n }})
866+  body := dcom {
867+    ->> {{ (X + Y) - ((X + Y) - Y) = n ∧ (X + Y) - Y = m }}
868+    X := X + Y {{ X - (X - Y) = n ∧ X - Y = m }};
869+    Y := X - Y {{ X - Y = n ∧ Y = m }};
870+    X := X - Y {{ X = n ∧ Y = m }}
871+  }
872+
873+theorem swap_correct (m n : Nat) :
874+    (swapDec m n).OuterTripleValid := by
875+  sorry
876+
877+-- And here is the formal decorated version of the "positive difference"
878+-- program from earlier:
879+
880+def positiveDifferenceDec : Decorated where
881+  pre := ({{ True }})
882+  body := dcom {
883+    if (X ≤ Y) then
884+      {{ True ∧ X ≤ Y }}
885+      ->> {{ (Y - X) + X = Y ∨ (Y - X) + Y = X }}
886+      Z := Y - X {{ Z + X = Y ∨ Z + Y = X }}
887+    else
888+      {{ True ∧ ¬ X ≤ Y }}
889+      ->> {{ (X - Y) + X = Y ∨ (X - Y) + Y = X }}
890+      Z := X - Y {{ Z + X = Y ∨ Z + Y = X }}
891+    end
892+      {{ Z + X = Y ∨ Z + Y = X }}
893+  }
894+
895+theorem positive_difference_correct :
896+    positiveDifferenceDec.OuterTripleValid := by
897+  sorry
898+
899+-- ### Exercise (2 stars): if_minus_plus_correct ⭐⭐
900+
901+-- Here is a skeleton of the formal decorated version of the `if_minus_plus`
902+-- program that we saw earlier. Replace all occurrences of `FILL_IN_HERE` with
903+-- appropriate assertions and fill in the proof (which should be just as
904+-- straightforward as in the examples above).
905+
906+def ifMinusPlusDec : Decorated where
907+  pre := ({{ True }})
908+  body := dcom {
909+    if (X ≤ Y) then
910+      {{ True ∧ X ≤ Y }}
911+      ->> {{ Y = X + (Y - X) }}
912+      Z := Y - X {{ Y = X + Z }}
913+    else
914+      {{ True ∧ ¬ X ≤ Y }}
915+      ->> {{ X + Z = X + Z }}
916+      Y := X + Z {{ Y = X + Z }}
917+    end
918+      {{ Y = X + Z }}
919+  }
920+
921+theorem if_minus_plus_correct :
922+    ifMinusPlusDec.OuterTripleValid := by
923+  sorry

925+-- ### Exercise (2 stars): div_mod_outer_triple_valid ⭐⭐
926+
927+-- Fill in appropriate assertions for the division program from above.
928+
929+def divModDec (a b : Nat) : Decorated where
930+  pre := ({{ True }})
931+  body := dcom {
932+    ->> {{ b * 0 + a = a }}
933+    X := ~(Aexp.num a) {{ b * 0 + X = a }};
934+    Y := 0 {{ b * Y + X = a }};
935+    while (~(Aexp.num b) ≤ X) do
936+      {{ b * Y + X = a ∧ b ≤ X }}
937+      ->> {{ b * (Y + 1) + (X - b) = a }}
938+      X := X - ~(Aexp.num b) {{ b * (Y + 1) + X = a }};
939+      Y := Y + 1 {{ b * Y + X = a }}
940+    end
941+      {{ b * Y + X = a ∧ ¬ b ≤ X }}
942+    ->> {{ b * Y + X = a ∧ X < b }}
943+  }
944+
945+theorem div_mod_outer_triple_valid (a b : Nat) :
946+    (divModDec a b).OuterTripleValid := by
947+  sorry

949+-- ## Finding Loop Invariants
950+
951+-- Once the outermost precondition and postcondition are chosen, the only
952+-- creative part of a verifying program using Hoare Logic is finding the right
953+-- loop invariants. The reason this is difficult is the same as the reason
954+-- that inductive mathematical proofs are:
955+
956+-- - Strengthening a *loop invariant* means that you have a stronger assumption
957+--   to work with when trying to establish the postcondition of the loop body,
958+--   but it also means that the loop body's postcondition is harder to prove.
959+
960+-- - Similarly, strengthening an *induction hypothesis* means that you have a
961+--   stronger assumption to work with when trying to complete the induction step
962+--   of the proof, but it also means that the statement being proved inductively
963+--   is harder to prove.
964+
965+-- This section explains how to approach the challenge of finding loop
966+-- invariants through a series of examples and exercises.
967+
968+-- ### Example: Slow Subtraction
969+
970+-- The following program subtracts the value of `X` from the value of `Y` by
971+-- repeatedly decrementing both `X` and `Y`. We want to verify its correctness
972+-- with respect to the pre- and postconditions shown:
973+
974+--   {{ X = m /\ Y = n }}
975+--     while X <> 0 do
976+--       Y := Y - 1;
977+--       X := X - 1
978+--     end
979+--   {{ Y = n - m }}
980+
981+-- To verify this program, we need to find an invariant `Inv` for the loop. As
982+-- a first step we can leave `Inv` as an unknown and build a *skeleton* for
983+-- the proof by applying the rules for local consistency, working from the end
984+-- of the program to the beginning, as usual, and without doing any thinking
985+-- at all yet.
986+
987+-- This leads to the following skeleton:
988+
989+--   (1)    {{ X = m /\ Y = n }}  ->>                   (a)
990+--   (2)    {{ Inv }}
991+--            while X <> 0 do
992+--   (3)              {{ Inv /\ X <> 0 }}  ->>          (c)
993+--   (4)              {{ Inv [X |-> X-1] [Y |-> Y-1] }}
994+--              Y := Y - 1;
995+--   (5)              {{ Inv [X |-> X-1] }}
996+--              X := X - 1
997+--   (6)              {{ Inv }}
998+--            end
999+--   (7)    {{ Inv /\ ~ (X <> 0) }}  ->>                (b)
1000+--   (8)    {{ Y = n - m }}
1001+
1002+-- Examining this skeleton, we can see that any valid `Inv` will have to
1003+-- respect three conditions:
1004+
1005+-- - (a) it must be *weak* enough to be implied by the loop's precondition,
1006+--   i.e., (1) must imply (2);
1007+
1008+-- - (b) it must be *strong* enough to imply the program's postcondition, i.e.,
1009+--   (7) must imply (8);
1010+
1011+-- - (c) it must be *preserved* by a single iteration of the loop, assuming that
1012+--   the loop guard also evaluates to true, i.e., (3) must imply (4).
1013+
1014+-- These conditions are actually independent of the particular program and
1015+-- specification we are considering: every loop invariant has to satisfy them.
1016+
1017+-- One way to find a loop invariant that simultaneously satisfies these three
1018+-- conditions is by using an iterative process: start with a "candidate"
1019+-- invariant (e.g., a guess or a heuristic choice) and check the three
1020+-- conditions above; if any of the checks fails, try to use the information
1021+-- that we get from the failure to produce another — hopefully better —
1022+-- candidate invariant, and repeat.
1023+
1024+-- For instance, in the reduce-to-zero example above, we saw that, for a very
1025+-- simple loop, choosing `True` as a loop invariant did the job. Maybe it will
1026+-- work here too. To find out, let's try instantiating `Inv` with `True` in
1027+-- the skeleton above and see what we get...
1028+
1029+--   (1)    {{ X = m /\ Y = n }} ->>                    (a - OK)
1030+--   (2)    {{ True }}
1031+--            while X <> 0 do
1032+--   (3)                   {{ True /\ X <> 0 }} ->>     (c - OK)
1033+--   (4)                   {{ True }}
1034+--              Y := Y - 1;
1035+--   (5)                   {{ True }}
1036+--              X := X - 1
1037+--   (6)                   {{ True }}
1038+--            end
1039+--   (7)    {{ True /\ ~(X <> 0) }} ->>                 (b - WRONG!)
1040+--   (8)    {{ Y = n - m }}
1041+
1042+-- While conditions (a) and (c) are trivially satisfied, (b) is wrong: it is
1043+-- not the case that `True /\ X = 0` (7) implies `Y = n - m` (8). In fact, the
1044+-- two assertions are completely unrelated, so it is very easy to find a
1045+-- counterexample to the implication (say, `Y = X = m = 0` and `n = 1`).
1046+
1047+-- If we want (b) to hold, we need to strengthen the loop invariant so that it
1048+-- implies the postcondition (8). One simple way to do this is to let the loop
1049+-- invariant *be* the postcondition. So let's return to our skeleton,
1050+-- instantiate `Inv` with `Y = n - m`, and try checking conditions (a) to (c)
1051+-- again.
1052+
1053+--   (1)    {{ X = m /\ Y = n }} ->>                        (a - WRONG!)
1054+--   (2)    {{ Y = n - m }}
1055+--            while X <> 0 do
1056+--   (3)                     {{ Y = n - m /\ X <> 0 }} ->>  (c - WRONG!)
1057+--   (4)                     {{ Y - 1 = n - m }}
1058+--              Y := Y - 1;
1059+--   (5)                     {{ Y = n - m }}
1060+--              X := X - 1
1061+--   (6)                     {{ Y = n - m }}
1062+--            end
1063+--   (7)    {{ Y = n - m /\ ~(X <> 0) }} ->>                (b - OK)
1064+--   (8)    {{ Y = n - m }}
1065+
1066+-- This time, condition (b) holds trivially, but (a) and (c) are broken.
1067+-- Condition (a) requires that (1) `X = m /\ Y = n` implies (2) `Y = n - m`.
1068+-- If we substitute `Y` by `n` we have to show that `n = n - m` for arbitrary
1069+-- `m` and `n`, which is not the case (for instance, when `m = n = 1`).
1070+-- Condition (c) requires that `n - m - 1 = n - m`, which fails, for instance,
1071+-- for `n = 1` and `m = 0`. So, although `Y = n - m` holds at the end of the
1072+-- loop, it does not hold from the start, and it doesn't hold on each
1073+-- iteration; it is not a correct loop invariant.
1074+
1075+-- This failure is not very surprising: the variable `Y` changes during the
1076+-- loop, while `m` and `n` are constant, so the assertion we chose didn't have
1077+-- much chance of being a loop invariant!
1078+
1079+-- To do better, we need to generalize (7) to some statement that is
1080+-- equivalent to (8) when `X` is `0`, since this will be the case when the
1081+-- loop terminates, and that "fills the gap" in some appropriate way when `X`
1082+-- is nonzero. Looking at how the loop works, we can observe that `X` and `Y`
1083+-- are decremented together until `X` reaches `0`. So, if `X = 2` and `Y = 5`
1084+-- initially, after one iteration of the loop we obtain `X = 1` and `Y = 4`;
1085+-- after two iterations `X = 0` and `Y = 3`; and then the loop stops. Notice
1086+-- that the difference between `Y` and `X` stays constant between iterations:
1087+-- initially, `Y = n` and `X = m`, and the difference is always `n - m`. So
1088+-- let's try instantiating `Inv` in the skeleton above with `Y - X = n - m`.
1089+
1090+--   (1)    {{ X = m /\ Y = n }} ->>                            (a - OK)
1091+--   (2)    {{ Y - X = n - m }}
1092+--            while X <> 0 do
1093+--   (3)                    {{ Y - X = n - m /\ X <> 0 }} ->>   (c - OK)
1094+--   (4)                    {{ (Y - 1) - (X - 1) = n - m }}
1095+--              Y := Y - 1;
1096+--   (5)                    {{ Y - (X - 1) = n - m }}
1097+--              X := X - 1
1098+--   (6)                    {{ Y - X = n - m }}
1099+--            end
1100+--   (7)    {{ Y - X = n - m /\ ~(X <> 0) }} ->>                (b - OK)
1101+--   (8)    {{ Y = n - m }}
1102+
1103+-- Success! Conditions (a), (b) and (c) all hold now. (To verify (c), we need
1104+-- to check that, under the assumption that `X <> 0`, we have
1105+-- `Y - X = (Y - 1) - (X - 1)`; this holds for all natural numbers `X` and
1106+-- `Y`.)
1107+
1108+-- Here is the final version of the decorated program:
1109+
1110+def subtractSlowlyDec (m n : Nat) : Decorated where
1111+  pre := ({{ X = m ∧ Y = n }})
1112+  body := dcom {
1113+    ->> {{ Y - X = n - m }}
1114+    while (X ≠ 0) do
1115+      {{ Y - X = n - m ∧ ¬ X = 0 }}
1116+      ->> {{ (Y - 1) - (X - 1) = n - m }}
1117+      Y := Y - 1 {{ Y - (X - 1) = n - m }};
1118+      X := X - 1 {{ Y - X = n - m }}
1119+    end
1120+      {{ Y - X = n - m ∧ X = 0 }}
1121+    ->> {{ Y = n - m }}
1122+  }
1123+
1124+theorem subtract_slowly_outer_triple_valid (m n : Nat) :
1125+    (subtractSlowlyDec m n).OuterTripleValid := by
1126+  sorry
1127+
1128+-- ### Exercise: Slow Assignment
1129+
1130+-- ### Exercise (2 stars): slow_assignment ⭐⭐
1131+
1132+-- A roundabout way of assigning a number currently stored in `X` to the
1133+-- variable `Y` is to start `Y` at `0`, then decrement `X` until it hits `0`,
1134+-- incrementing `Y` at each step. Here is a program that implements this idea.
1135+-- Fill in decorations and prove the decorated program correct. (The proof
1136+-- should be very simple.)
1137+
1138+def slowAssignmentDec (m : Nat) : Decorated where
1139+  pre := ({{ X = m }})
1140+  body := dcom {
1141+    Y := 0 {{ sorry }};
1142+    (->> {{ sorry }}
1143+      while (X ≠ 0) do
1144+        {{ sorry }}
1145+        ->> {{ sorry }}
1146+        X := X - 1 {{ sorry }};
1147+        (->> {{ sorry }}
1148+          Y := Y + 1 {{ sorry }})
1149+      end
1150+        {{ sorry }}
1151+      ->> {{ Y = m }})
1152+  }
1153+
1154+theorem slow_assignment (m : Nat) :
1155+    (slowAssignmentDec m).OuterTripleValid := by
1156+  sorry
1157+
1158+-- ### Example: Parity
1159+
1160+-- Here is a cute way of computing the parity of a value initially stored in
1161+-- `X`, due to Daniel Cristofani.
1162+
1163+--   {{ X = m }}
1164+--     while 2 <= X do
1165+--       X := X - 2
1166+--     end
1167+--   {{ X = parity m }}
1168+
1169+-- The `parity` function used in the specification is defined in Lean as
1170+-- follows:
1171+
1172+def parity : Nat → Nat
1173+  | 0 => 0
1174+  | 1 => 1
1175+  | Nat.succ (Nat.succ n) => parity n
1176+
1177+-- The postcondition does not hold at the beginning of the loop, since
1178+-- `m = parity m` does not hold for an arbitrary `m`, so we cannot hope to use
1179+-- that as a loop invariant. To find a loop invariant that works, let's think
1180+-- a bit about what this loop does. On each iteration it decrements `X` by
1181+-- `2`, which preserves the parity of `X`. So the parity of `X` does not
1182+-- change, i.e., it is invariant. The initial value of `X` is `m`, so the
1183+-- parity of `X` is always equal to the parity of `m`. Using
1184+-- `parity X = parity m` as an invariant we obtain the following decorated
1185+-- program:
1186+
1187+--   {{ X = m }} ->>                                         (a - OK)
1188+--   {{ parity X = parity m }}
1189+--     while 2 <= X do
1190+--                  {{ parity X = parity m /\ 2 <= X }} ->>  (c - OK)
1191+--                  {{ parity (X-2) = parity m }}
1192+--       X := X - 2
1193+--                  {{ parity X = parity m }}
1194+--     end
1195+--   {{ parity X = parity m /\ ~(2 <= X) }} ->>              (b - OK)
1196+--   {{ X = parity m }}
1197+
1198+-- With this loop invariant, conditions (a), (b), and (c) are all satisfied.
1199+-- For verifying (b), we observe that, when `X < 2`, we have `parity X = X`
1200+-- (we can easily see this in the definition of `parity`). For verifying (c),
1201+-- we observe that, when `2 <= X`, we have `parity X = parity (X-2)`.
1202+
1203+-- ### Exercise (3 stars): parity ⭐⭐⭐
1204+
1205+-- Translate the above informal decorated program into a formal one and prove
1206+-- it correct.
1207+
1208+-- Hint: There are actually several possible loop invariants that all lead to
1209+-- good proofs; one that leads to a particularly simple proof is
1210+-- `parity X = parity m`. Ordinary Lean functions can be applied directly to
1211+-- Imp variables inside assertions, so this can be written as
1212+-- `{{ parity X = parity m }}`.
1213+
1214+def parityDec (m : Nat) : Decorated where
1215+  pre := ({{ X = m }})
1216+  body :=
1217+    let inv : Assertion :=
1218+      sorry
1219+    let guardedInv : Assertion :=
1220+      sorry
1221+    let bodyPre : Assertion :=
1222+      sorry
1223+    let exit : Assertion :=
1224+      sorry
1225+    let post : Assertion :=
1226+      fun st => st X = parity m
1227+    dcom {
1228+    ->> {{ inv }}
1229+    while (2 ≤ X) do
1230+      {{ guardedInv }}
1231+      ->> {{ bodyPre }}
1232+      X := X - 2 {{ inv }}
1233+    end
1234+      {{ exit }}
1235+    ->> {{ post }}
1236+  }
1237+
1238+-- If you use the suggested loop invariant, you may find the following two
1239+-- lemmas helpful.
1240+
1241+theorem parity_ge_2 (x : Nat) (h : 2 ≤ x) :
1242+    parity (x - 2) = parity x := by
1243+  sorry
1244+
1245+theorem parity_lt_2 (x : Nat) (h : ¬ 2 ≤ x) :
1246+    parity x = x := by
1247+  sorry
1248+
1249+theorem parity_outer_triple_valid (m : Nat) :
1250+    (parityDec m).OuterTripleValid := by
1251+  sorry
1252+
1253+-- FILL IN HERE
1254+
1255+-- ### Example: Finding Square Roots
1256+
1257+-- The following program computes the integer square root of `X` by naive
1258+-- iteration:
1259+
1260+--   {{ X=m }}
1261+--     Z := 0;
1262+--     while (Z+1)*(Z+1) <= X do
1263+--       Z := Z+1
1264+--     end
1265+--   {{ Z*Z<=m /\ m<(Z+1)*(Z+1) }}
1266+
1267+-- WORK IN CLASS
1268+
1269+-- As we did before, we can try to use the postcondition as a candidate loop
1270+-- invariant, obtaining the following decorated program:
1271+
1272+--   (1)  {{ X=m }} ->>                  (a - second conjunct of (2) WRONG!)
1273+--   (2)  {{ 0*0 <= m /\ m<(0+1)*(0+1) }}
1274+--           Z := 0
1275+--   (3)            {{ Z*Z <= m /\ m<(Z+1)*(Z+1) }};
1276+--           while (Z+1)*(Z+1) <= X do
1277+--   (4)            {{ Z*Z<=m /\ m<(Z+1)*(Z+1)
1278+--                            /\ (Z+1)*(Z+1)<=X }} ->>          (c - WRONG!)
1279+--   (5)            {{ (Z+1)*(Z+1)<=m /\ m<((Z+1)+1)*((Z+1)+1) }}
1280+--             Z := Z+1
1281+--   (6)            {{ Z*Z<=m /\ m<(Z+1)*(Z+1) }}
1282+--           end
1283+--   (7)  {{ Z*Z<=m /\ m<(Z+1)*(Z+1) /\ ~((Z+1)*(Z+1)<=X) }} ->>    (b - OK)
1284+--   (8)  {{ Z*Z<=m /\ m<(Z+1)*(Z+1) }}
1285+
1286+-- This didn't work very well: conditions (a) and (c) both failed. Looking at
1287+-- condition (c), we see that the second conjunct of (4) is almost the same as
1288+-- the first conjunct of (5), except that (4) mentions `X` while (5) mentions
1289+-- `m`. But note that `X` is never assigned in this program, so we should
1290+-- always have `X=m`. We didn't propagate this information from (1) into the
1291+-- loop invariant, but we could!
1292+
1293+-- Also, we don't need the second conjunct of (8), since we can obtain it from
1294+-- the negation of the guard — the third conjunct in (7) — again under the
1295+-- assumption that `X=m`. This allows us to simplify a bit.
1296+
1297+-- So we now try `X=m /\ Z*Z <= m` as the loop invariant:
1298+
1299+--   {{ X=m }} ->>                                           (a - OK)
1300+--   {{ X=m /\ 0*0 <= m }}
1301+--     Z := 0
1302+--                {{ X=m /\ Z*Z <= m }};
1303+--     while (Z+1)*(Z+1) <= X do
1304+--                {{ X=m /\ Z*Z<=m /\ (Z+1)*(Z+1)<=X }} ->>  (c - OK)
1305+--                {{ X=m /\ (Z+1)*(Z+1)<=m }}
1306+--       Z := Z + 1
1307+--                {{ X=m /\ Z*Z<=m }}
1308+--     end
1309+--   {{ X=m /\ Z*Z<=m /\ ~((Z+1)*(Z+1)<=X) }} ->>            (b - OK)
1310+--   {{ Z*Z<=m /\ m<(Z+1)*(Z+1) }}
1311+
1312+-- This works, since conditions (a), (b), and (c) are now all rather trivially
1313+-- satisfied.
1314+
1315+-- Very often, when a variable is used in a loop in a read-only fashion (i.e.,
1316+-- it is referred to by the program or by the specification, and it is not
1317+-- changed by the loop), it is necessary to record the *fact* that it doesn't
1318+-- change in the loop invariant.
1319+
1320+-- ### Exercise (3 stars): sqrt ⭐⭐⭐
1321+
1322+-- Translate the above informal decorated program into a formal one and prove
1323+-- it correct.
1324+
1325+-- Hint: The loop invariant here must ensure that `Z*Z` is consistently less
1326+-- than or equal to X.
1327+
1328+def sqrtDec (m : Nat) : Decorated where
1329+  pre := ({{ X = m }})
1330+  body := dcom {
1331+    ->> {{ sorry }}
1332+    Z := 0 {{ sorry }};
1333+    while ((Z + 1) * (Z + 1) ≤ X) do
1334+      {{ sorry }}
1335+      ->> {{ sorry }}
1336+      Z := Z + 1 {{ sorry }}
1337+    end
1338+      {{ sorry }}
1339+    ->> {{ Z * Z ≤ m ∧ m < (Z + 1) * (Z + 1) }}
1340+  }
1341+
1342+theorem sqrt_correct (m : Nat) :
1343+    (sqrtDec m).OuterTripleValid := by
1344+  sorry
1345+
1346+-- ### Example: Squaring
1347+
1348+-- Here is a program that squares `X` by repeated addition:
1349+
1350+--   {{ X = m }}
1351+--     Y := 0;
1352+--     Z := 0;
1353+--     while Y <> X  do
1354+--       Z := Z + X;
1355+--       Y := Y + 1
1356+--     end
1357+--   {{ Z = m*m }}
1358+
1359+-- WORK IN CLASS
1360+
1361+-- The first thing to note is that the loop reads `X` but doesn't change its
1362+-- value. As we saw in the previous example, it can be a good idea in such
1363+-- cases to add `X = m` to the loop invariant. The other thing that we know is
1364+-- often useful in the loop invariant is the postcondition, so let's add that
1365+-- too, leading to the candidate loop invariant `Z = m * m /\ X = m`.
1366+
1367+--   {{ X = m }} ->>                                       (a - WRONG)
1368+--   {{ 0 = m*m /\ X = m }}
1369+--     Y := 0
1370+--                  {{ 0 = m*m /\ X = m }};
1371+--     Z := 0
1372+--                  {{ Z = m*m /\ X = m }};
1373+--     while Y <> X do
1374+--                  {{ Z = m*m /\ X = m /\ Y <> X }} ->>   (c - WRONG)
1375+--                  {{ Z+X = m*m /\ X = m }}
1376+--       Z := Z + X
1377+--                  {{ Z = m*m /\ X = m }};
1378+--       Y := Y + 1
1379+--                  {{ Z = m*m /\ X = m }}
1380+--     end
1381+--   {{ Z = m*m /\ X = m /\ ~(Y <> X) }} ->>               (b - OK)
1382+--   {{ Z = m*m }}
1383+
1384+-- Conditions (a) and (c) fail because of the `Z = m*m` part. While `Z` starts
1385+-- at `0` and works itself up to `m*m`, we can't expect `Z` to be `m*m` from
1386+-- the start. If we look at how `Z` progresses in the loop, after the 1st
1387+-- iteration `Z = m`, after the 2nd iteration `Z = 2*m`, and at the end
1388+-- `Z = m*m`. Since the variable `Y` tracks how many times we go through the
1389+-- loop, this leads us to derive a new loop invariant candidate:
1390+-- `Z = Y*m /\ X = m`.
1391+
1392+--   {{ X = m }} ->>                                        (a - OK)
1393+--   {{ 0 = 0*m /\ X = m }}
1394+--     Y := 0
1395+--                   {{ 0 = Y*m /\ X = m }};
1396+--     Z := 0
1397+--                   {{ Z = Y*m /\ X = m }};
1398+--     while Y <> X do
1399+--                   {{ Z = Y*m /\ X = m /\ Y <> X }} ->>   (c - OK)
1400+--                   {{ Z+X = (Y+1)*m /\ X = m }}
1401+--       Z := Z + X
1402+--                   {{ Z = (Y+1)*m /\ X = m }};
1403+--       Y := Y + 1
1404+--                   {{ Z = Y*m /\ X = m }}
1405+--     end
1406+--   {{ Z = Y*m /\ X = m /\ ~(Y <> X) }} ->>                (b - OK)
1407+--   {{ Z = m*m }}
1408+
1409+-- This new loop invariant makes the proof go through: all three conditions
1410+-- are easy to check.
1411+
1412+-- It is worth comparing the postcondition `Z = m*m` and the `Z = Y*m`
1413+-- conjunct of the loop invariant. It is often the case that one has to
1414+-- replace parameters with variables — or with expressions involving both
1415+-- variables and parameters, like `m - Y` — when going from postconditions to
1416+-- loop invariants.

1418+-- ### Exercise: Factorial

1420+-- ### Exercise (4 stars): factorial_correct (Advanced) ⭐⭐⭐⭐
1421+
1422+-- Recall that `n!` denotes the factorial of `n` (i.e., `n! =
1423+-- 1*2*...*n`). We
1424+-- can define the factorial function recursively in Lean as follows:
1425+
1426+def fact : Nat → Nat
1427+  | 0 => 1
1428+  | Nat.succ n => Nat.succ n * fact n
1429+
1430+#eval fact 5
1431+
1432+-- First, write the Imp program `factorial` that calculates the factorial of
1433+-- the number initially stored in the variable `X` and puts it in the variable
1434+-- `Y`.

1440+
1441+-- Fill in the blanks and finish the proof of correctness. Bear in mind that
1442+-- we are working with natural numbers, for which both division and

1444+-- operations from your loop invariant is advisable!
1445+
1446+-- Then state a theorem named `factorial_correct` that says `factorialDec` is

1448+-- with just two subgoals, each of which requires establishing some
1449+-- mathematical property of `fact`, rather than proving anything about your

1452+-- Hint: if those two subgoals become tedious to prove, give some thought to

1454+-- are more amenable to manipulation in Lean. For example, recall that
1455+-- `1 + ...` is easier to work with than `... + 1`.

1457+def factorialDec (m : Nat) : Decorated := sorry
1458+
1459+theorem fact_sub_one (m : Nat) (h : m ≠ 0) :
1460+    m * fact (m - 1) = fact m := by
1461+  sorry
1462+
1463+theorem factorial_correct (m : Nat) :
1464+    (factorialDec m).OuterTripleValid := by
1465+  sorry

1697+    let afterZ : Assertion :=
