1740+-- ## Weakest Preconditions (Optional)
1741+
1742+-- Some preconditions are more interesting than others. For example, the Hoare
1743+-- triple
1744+
1745+--   {{ False }}  X := Y + 1  {{ X <= 5 }}
1746+
1747+-- is *not* very interesting: although it is perfectly valid, it tells us
1748+-- nothing useful. Since the precondition isn't satisfied by any state, it
1749+-- doesn't describe any situations where we can use the command `X := Y + 1`
1750+-- to achieve the postcondition `X <= 5`.
1751+
1752+-- By contrast,
1753+
1754+--   {{ Y <= 4 /\ Z = 0 }}  X := Y + 1 {{ X <= 5 }}
1755+
1756+-- has a useful precondition: it tells us that, if we can somehow create a
1757+-- situation in which we know that `Y <= 4 /\ Z = 0`, then running this
1758+-- command will produce a state satisfying the postcondition. However, this
1759+-- precondition is not as useful as it could be, because the `Z = 0` clause in
1760+-- the precondition actually has nothing to do with the postcondition
1761+-- `X <= 5`.
1762+
1763+-- The *most* useful precondition for this command is this one:
1764+
1765+--   {{ Y <= 4 }}  X := Y + 1  {{ X <= 5 }}
1766+
1767+-- The assertion `Y <= 4` is called the *weakest precondition* of `X := Y + 1`
1768+-- with respect to the postcondition `X <= 5`.
1769+
1770+-- Assertion `Y <= 4` is a *weakest precondition* of command `X := Y + 1` with
1771+-- respect to postcondition `X <= 5`. Think of *weakest* here as meaning
1772+-- "easiest to satisfy": a weakest precondition is one that as many states as
1773+-- possible can satisfy.
1774+
1775+-- `P` is a weakest precondition of command `c` for postcondition `Q` if
1776+
1777+-- - `P` is a precondition, that is, `{{P}} c {{Q}}`; and
1778+
1779+-- - `P` is at least as weak as all other preconditions, that is, if
1780+--   `{{P'}} c {{Q}}` then `P' ->> P`.
1781+
1782+-- Note that weakest preconditions need not be unique. For example, `Y <= 4`
1783+-- was a weakest precondition above, but so are the logically equivalent
1784+-- assertions `Y < 5`, `Y <= 2 * 2`, etc. It is easy to show that any two
1785+-- weakest preconditions `P` and `P'` of a command `c` with respect to
1786+-- postcondition `Q` are logically equivalent; that is, `P <<->> P'`.
1787+
1788+def IsWp (P : Assertion) (c : Com) (Q : Assertion) : Prop :=
1789+  ValidHoareTriple P c Q ∧
1790+  ∀ P' : Assertion, ValidHoareTriple P' c Q → P' ->> P
1791+
1792+-- ### Exercise (1 star): wp ⭐
1793+
1794+-- What are weakest preconditions of the following commands for the following
1795+-- postconditions?
1796+
1797+--   1) {{ ? }}  skip  {{ X = 5 }}
1798+
1799+--   2) {{ ? }}  X := Y + Z {{ X = 5 }}
1800+
1801+--   3) {{ ? }}  X := Y  {{ X = Y }}
1802+
1803+--   4) {{ ? }}
1804+--    if X = 0 then Y := Z + 1 else Y := W + 2 end
1805+--    {{ Y = 5 }}
1806+
1807+--   5) {{ ? }}
1808+--    X := 5
1809+--    {{ X = 0 }}
1810+
1811+--   6) {{ ? }}
1812+--    while true do X := 0 end
1813+--    {{ X = 0 }}
1814+
1815+-- ### Exercise (3 stars): is_wp (Advanced) ⭐⭐⭐
1816+
1817+-- Prove formally, using the definition of `ValidHoareTriple`, that `Y <= 4`
1818+-- is indeed a weakest precondition of `X := Y + 1` with respect to
1819+-- postcondition `X <= 5`.
1820+
1821+theorem is_wp_example :
1822+    IsWp ({{ Y ≤ 4 }}) (imp {X := Y + 1;})
1823+      ({{ X ≤ 5 }}) := by
1824+  sorry
1825+

1827+
1828+-- Show that the precondition in the rule `hoare_asgn` is in fact the weakest
1829+-- precondition.
1830+
1831+theorem hoare_asgn_weakest
1832+    (Q : Assertion) (x : Ident) (a : Aexp) :
1833+    IsWp (Assertion.sub x a Q) (imp {x := ~a;}) Q := by
1834+  sorry
1835+
1836+-- ### Exercise (2 stars): hoare_havoc_weakest (Advanced) ⭐⭐
1837+
1838+-- Show that your `havoc_pre` function from the `himp_hoare` exercise in the
1839+-- Hoare chapter returns a weakest precondition.
1840+
1841+namespace Himp2

1843+theorem hoare_havoc_weakest (P Q : Assertion) (x : Ident)
1844+    (h : Himp.ValidHoareTriple P (Himp.Com.havoc x) Q) :
1845+    P ->> Himp.havoc_pre x Q := by
1846+  sorry
1847+
1848+end Himp2

204+-- We make it a little easier to write Imp programs using normal constructors
205+-- (i.e., without notation), by using *implicit coercions*. In Lean, a `Coe`
206+-- instance tells the elaborator how to turn a value of one type into another
207+-- automatically:
208+
209+-- - `Coe Ident Aexp` lets us write a bare variable (an `Ident`) where an `Aexp`
210+--   is expected; the identifier is implicitly wrapped with `id`.
211+
212+-- - `OfNat Aexp n` lets us write a numeric literal where an `Aexp` is expected;
213+--   it is implicitly wrapped with `num`.
214+
215+-- - `Coe Bool Bexp` lets us write a boolean literal (`true`/`false`) where a
216+--   `Bexp` is expected; it is implicitly wrapped with `bool`.
217+
218+instance : Coe Ident Aexp where
219+  coe := .id
220+
221+instance (n : Nat) : OfNat Aexp n where
222+  ofNat := .num n
223+
224+instance : Coe Bool Bexp where
225+  coe := .bool
226+
227+-- With these coercions we can write `.plus 3 (.mult X 2)` instead of the
228+-- fully explicit `.plus (.num 3) (.mult (.id "X") (.num 2))`, and
229+-- `.and true (.not …)` instead of `.and (.bool true) (.not …)`. More readably
230+-- still, the concrete syntax from the Notations section lets us write these
231+-- examples directly:
232+
233+def example_aexp : Aexp := aexp { 3 + (X * 2) }
234+def example_bexp : Bexp := bexp { true ∧ ¬(X ≤ 4) }

250-/-- In Lean, "inversion" on `leq : f n ≤ 0`, where `f : Nat → Nat`,
251-  requires `generalizing e : f n = m`, since Lean does not perform
252-  the dependent case analysis automatically. `cases leq` will fail here.
253-  We want to keep the style of reasoning familiar to PL:
254-  "I know `h`; what must have been true for `h` to be true?"
255-  The technicality of needing to generalize hinders teaching and learning
256-  this style of reasoning for audiences new to proof assistants and logic.
257-  To solve this, we introduce and use the `inversion` tactic,
258-  which automatically generalizes varaibles, performs case analysis,
259-  and eliminates impossible subcases. -/

7976 -- explicitly, Lean searches for one and provides it on its own. We specify

8178 -- function as a field; a `class` is like an interface in Java or a trait in
82--- Rust. Particular implementations of that class are called *instance*; each
83--- type can have its own instance of a class. For functions that would use
84--- such instances, we specify the name of the class in a *instance implicit*
85--- on the polymorphic variable that the instance's function applies to. This
86--- directs Lean to rely on the class inside the function, and to find and fill
87--- in the appropriate instance when the function is called.

374-namespace Algebra
375-
376--- This facility is very powerful, and is used extensively in Lean to define
377--- mathematical structures that carry both operators and laws about how those
378--- operators interact. As a simple example, let's use a typeclass to define a
379--- *monoid*, a simple algebraic structure that includes four things:
380-
381--- - an underlying set of data, represented by a type `α`,
382-
383--- - an operator (which we'll write `⊗`, typed otimes) that combines two
384---   elements of type `α` into one,
385-
386--- - a particular element `id` of type `α`, which we call the "identity
387---   element", and
388-
389--- - some laws about the interaction of `⊗` and `id`, namely that:
390-
391---   - `∀ x, id ⊗ x = x = x ⊗ id`, and
392---   - `∀ x y z, x ⊗ (y ⊗ z) = (x ⊗ y) ⊗ z` (i.e., that `⊗` is associative)
393-
394--- We can express these requirements in the form of a typeclass:
395-
396--- first we define a notation typeclass for our operator ⊗
397-class OpSet (α : Type) where
398-  op : α → α → α
399-
400-infixr:70 " ⊗ " => OpSet.op
401-
402-class Monoid (α : Type) extends (OpSet α) where
403-  id : α
404-  left_id : ∀ (x : α), id ⊗ x = x
405-  right_id : ∀ (x : α), x ⊗ id = x
406-  assoc : ∀ (x y z : α), x ⊗ (y ⊗ z) = (x ⊗ y) ⊗ z
407-
408--- The `extends` keyword indicates that the `Monoid` typeclass extends the
409--- `OpSet` typeclass, which just defines a set with an operator and some
410--- notation for it. The `Monoid` typeclass "inherits" the fields of `OpSet`,
411--- similar to how a class would in an object-oriented language.
412-
413--- As one might expect, the `+` operator over `Nat`s forms a monoid, where `0`
414--- is the identity element. Note that we don't have to define `Nat`'s `OpSet`
415--- instance separately, we can define a single instance that implements both
416--- classes.
417-
418-instance : Monoid Nat where
419-  op := Nat.add
420-  id := 0
421-  left_id := by lia
422-  right_id := by lia
423-  assoc := by lia

438-
439--- There are also many monoids over other types. Most usefully in computer
440--- science, lists of any type also form a monoid, with `List.append` as the
441--- operator in question:
442-

445-  id := sorry
446-  left_id := sorry
447-  right_id := sorry
448-  assoc := sorry
449-
450--- In addition to defining instances of `Monoid`, we can also prove some
451--- properties about monoids in general, just based on the laws defined on the
452--- typeclass. One simple theorem about monoids is that the identity element of
453--- a monoid is unique. That is, if we have two monoids over the same set with
454--- the same operator, their identity elements must also be the same:
455-
456-theorem id_unique {α : Type} {m₁ m₂ : Monoid α} (h : m₁.op = m₂.op) : m₁.id = m₂.id := by
457-  obtain @⟨op₁, id₁, left_id₁, right_id₁, assoc₁⟩ := m₁
458-  obtain @⟨op₂, id₂, left_id₂, right_id₂, assoc₂⟩ := m₂
459-  have h' : id₁ = id₂ := by
460-    -- this introduces a use of m₁'s operator
461-    rw [← left_id₁ id₂]
462-    -- we use our hypothesis to rewrite m₁'s operator into m₂'s
463-    rw [h]
464-    -- then, we can use m₂'s right id
465-    rw [right_id₂]
466-  -- the goal `m₁.id = m₂.id` is equivalent with `id₁ = id₂` even though it displays `Monoid.id = Monoid.id`
467-  exact h'
468-
469--- In the above proof, we can destructure the monoid instances `m₁` and `m₂`
470--- with the `obtain` tactic we saw in the Logic chapter. When we do so
471--- however, because these are class instances instead of normal structures, we
472--- preface our tuple with the `@` symbol. When stepping through the above
473--- proof, if the notation is confusing to you, remember that you can set
474--- `set_option pp.all true` or `set_option pp.explicit true` to make Lean show
475--- you more clearly what is going on. For example, the goal is displayed as
476--- `Monoid.id = Monoid.id` since the instances `m₁` and `m₂` are implicit
477--- arguments to `Monoid.id`. Setting `pp.explicit true` displays the goal as
478--- `@Eq α (@Monoid.id α m₁) (@Monoid.id α m₂)`.

608+--     [Meta.Tactic.simp.rewrite] apply_eq_getElem:1000:
609+--           m[a]

612+--     [Meta.Tactic.simp.rewrite] apply_eq_getElem:1000:
613+--           (MyGetElem.getElem m)[a]
614+--         ==>

616+--     [Meta.Tactic.simp.rewrite] apply_eq_getElem:1000:
617+--           (MyGetElem.getElem (MyGetElem.getElem m))[a]
618+--         ==>
619+--           (MyGetElem.getElem (MyGetElem.getElem (MyGetElem.getElem m)))[a]
620+--     [Meta.Tactic.simp.rewrite] apply_eq_getElem:1000:
621+--           (MyGetElem.getElem (MyGetElem.getElem (MyGetElem.getElem m)))[a]
622+--         ==>...`
623+--
624+--     So I think the issue here is that the LHS m a is too board, causing
625+--     this lemma repeating itself. First we have `m a => m[a], but m[a]` is
626+--     defeq to (MyGetElem.getElem m) a, and nevertheless we require m to be a
627+--     TotalMap, a TotalMap is defeq to α → β. So this lemma applies again --
628+--     `(MyGetElem.getElem m) a => (MyGetElem.getElem m)[a]` which is
629+--     `(MyGetElem.getElem (MyGetElem.getElem m))[a]` and keep going.
